en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Essential Practice of Relinquishing the Body.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at [blank] together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, with the Great Bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa serving as their leader.
One thousand [monks] were present together,
with the flying-ascendant pratyekabuddhas as their leaders.
Eight thousand great bodhisattvas were also present together.
With Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva as the leader,
there were the Great Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, the Four Great Kings, the nāgas and spirits of the eight classes,
and the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst this assembly, smiled with joy.
He emitted a great radiance that illuminated the Śītavana cemetery and this great gathering.
Before long, the light returned and entered through his mouth.
He sat with his body upright,
established in right mindfulness and unmoving.
At that time, Kāśyapa rose from his seat.
Baring his right shoulder,
he circumambulated [the Buddha] three times and then knelt with his right knee on the ground before the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,
for what reason does the Tathāgata smile with joy amidst this assembly?"
He emitted a great radiance that illuminated the śmaśāna and this great assembly.
Before long, the light returned and entered back through his mouth;
he then sat with his body upright.
With right mindfulness unmoving, he made this wish: "I pray that the Tathāgata will explain his resolve.
The Buddha said:
Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
I shall explain the essential Dharma for you.
With my Buddha-eye, I behold this forest:
those who practice the relinquishing of the body shall in the future attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
If there are sentient beings who can conceive the superior intention to sacrifice their bodies,
giving rise to a mind of equanimity free from love and hatred,
and without engendering stinginess;
If one can give rise to this mind even once,
although they have not yet cast off the body, that person has already surpassed the practice of the two vehicles by hundreds of thousands of millions of times;
they are then equal to all the bodhisattvas and those of like resolve.
How much more so when one sacrifices body and life for the sake of all sentient beings;
such merit as this would be inexhaustible were I to describe it in full.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as for what the Tathāgata has said regarding being present in the śītavana charnel ground and reaching all sentient beings—this meaning is not so; it cannot be called 'universal'."
"If it were universal, then sentient beings of the water-element would have no distinct portions.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will show me the meaning of 'universal'.
The Buddha said:
"Good son, I have just granted permission for you to speak, and you have immediately asked:
'If there are sentient beings who are able to give away their own bodies...'"
It was divided into two parts:
one part in the water and one part on land.
When this person’s life is about to end,
they shall entrust their body to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who shares their same aspiration, requesting that it be divided into two parts.
The merit obtained by these emanations is no different from the merit of the person who sacrificed their own body.
I recall the time of the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
While practicing the path to enlightenment in Śrāvastī,
he vowed to sacrifice his body, life, skin, flesh, sinews, and bones,
with each thought succeeding the next in an uninterrupted stream.
At that time, Maitreya will be my good friend;
when my life has come to an end, he will immediately divide it into two parts and enshrine them according to the Dharma.
Maitreya joined his palms and made this vow:
"May these humble offerings serve as the condition for all sentient beings—those who travel by water, land, or air—to partake of food.
By virtue of this merit, may we encounter one another from time immemorial and remain as kinsmen."
Next, he will become a Buddha; he is that very person.
Because of this, I sacrificed my body and made a great vow:
"If there are sentient beings who, out of hunger, eat my flesh..."
"Drink my blood! Having drunk and eaten it, may all sentient beings,
by virtue of consuming my flesh, give rise to the bodhicitta and be freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst."
In the future, you shall obtain the food of the joy of Dharma and so forth to sustain your *svābhāvikakāya*.
Those who drink my blood shall be freed from all thirst for craving.
One shall then receive the infusion of the water of Dharma into the source of the mind;
by cherishing the King of Dharma and relying upon the transformation body,
one will, for this reason, swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, when I was on the path of practice and first generated the mind of enlightenment,
it was during my fourth birth— after having died and been reborn three times—
that I was able to generate equanimity and freedom from craving.
During the time of the Buddha Śūnyatā-rāja,
as the Prince Sattva who had realized the principle of emptiness,
he offered his own body to a starving tigress to feed her seven cubs.
He was also King Candraprabha,
who extensively benefited thousands of heads; he was also Prince Danta.
He gave his wife and children as alms;
likewise, out of the power of loving-kindness and compassion, King Karuṇābala gave his own body to five yakṣas for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
On the slopes of the Snowy Mountains, I sought even half a verse by offering my own body as food for a rākṣasa.
If I were to speak at length of my births since beginningless time...
One could not exhaustively describe the relinquishing of body and life throughout hundreds of thousands of eons.
Why is this? It is because, in every case, one relinquishes the body through death at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta on the causal ground.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, although such persons as these perform the immeasurable merit of sacrificing their bodies,
I am not certain whether they have committed many transgressions throughout numerous previous lifetimes prior to making this offering."
"Will the karmic retribution for evil deeds committed in previous lives be extinguished by the merit gained upon casting off this body?
The Buddha said, "Good son,"
If there are sentient beings who frequently commit acts of killing against all other sentient beings throughout the Sahā world-system,
and who commit the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or slander the Vaipulya sutras;
Even down to devouring the flesh and blood of sentient beings—
such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless.
If there were a sentient being capable of giving their own body parts to universally relieve all sentient beings...
The suffering of hunger and thirst is removed,
and all such transgressions as described above are entirely extinguished.
All calamities and faults from time immemorial are swiftly eliminated without remainder.
Because one has relinquished the body, this is itself a great confession characterized by complete sincerity and shame.
All Buddhas of the ten directions together praise it. Good son!

Suppose there is a person who, since beginningless time, has committed such offenses as stealing the property of the Saṃgha, the property of the resident monks, or the property of the monks present before them; preaching the Dharma impurely;
using oversized measuring cups and heavy scales; and so forth.
They should enter the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts,
unable to attain liberation for hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
fearing they will incur future suffering, one should immediately request them to assemble.
In the Sahā world, all the great arhats— whether ordinary or noble— who possess the three knowledges and six supernormal powers and are endowed with the eight liberations,
as well as all the monks and nuns, gather together in one place.
Even if one wishes to extinguish their transgressions, they cannot be extinguished.
For this reason, there are hundreds of thousands of Gaṅgā-Saṃkha worlds,
and the entire assembly of the pure ocean-like Sangha does not gather together.
Because of these causes and conditions, such offenses are difficult to eradicate.
For this reason, it is called "the property of the Sangha that abides eternally," which belongs universally to the entire Dharma-realm, from the Buddhas above down to the śrāmaṇeras below.
All have their respective portions, yet they are not like those who,
in every place of birth,
vow to relinquish this body’s skin, flesh, sinews, and bones.
The offenses of the successive states of mind, as described above,
shall all be completely extinguished.
All records in the registers of the Celestial Bureaus and the Netherworld Offices shall naturally be erased.
For this reason, because I see such benefit,
I exhort all sentient beings that they should give their own bodies as an act of generosity, for they will certainly attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Maitreya, you and others must protect and uphold such sutras as these."
"May it be widely proclaimed and spread throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
In the evil age after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to a courageous and resolute mind.
I shall give my body as an offering for the sake of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) for all sentient beings;
such persons as these, I shall cause to attain liberation at the very beginning of the Dragon Flower Assembly.
I only pray that the Buddha will say:
"Have no further concern.
Great Brahmā Devānām-Indra, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
The eight classes of nāgas and devas, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās,
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,..."
For such persons as these,
we shall from now on provide protection,
ensuring that no one causes them any hindrance.
Why is this? Because such individuals will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One,
what should this be called?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
This sūtra is titled *The Sūtra on the Merit of Sacrificing the Body: The Essential Practice of All Buddhas*.
At that time, all devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Vow for the Sacrifice of the Body from the *Buddhabhāṣita-āvaśyaka-dehaparityāga-sūtra*. May all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time bear witness.
Disciple [Name], and others.
From beginningless time through this present life until the end of the future,
they have constantly offered both internal and external wealth as gifts while alive and as gifts at death.
Now that this disciple, so-and-so, has reached the end of this present life...
Furthermore, one gives the body of segmented birth—
its flesh, blood, skin, bones, head, eyes, marrow, brain,
as well as its hands and feet— to all hungry sentient beings.
To repay his past debts and to emulate the traces of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices,
he gave up his own flesh and blood and proceeded to the Śītavana cemetery.
The roots of goodness from the body that have been relinquished, those already accumulated,
and those yet to be accumulated— all present roots of goodness—
are dedicated through this virtuous aspiration for all sentient beings, in every place of their births and rebirths.
They do not give rise to craving or attachment toward their bodies, lives, or wealth;
they abandon what is false and return to what is correct,
and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
May they forever eliminate the three obstacles,
forever be free from poverty,
and constantly behold all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
